RDSP withdrawals: separate the beneficiary’s payment from assistance repaid to government

Follow a hypothetical permitted RDSP payment through the ordinary proportional repayment rule, then reconcile the cash leaving the plan and the value that remains.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 25 October 2026 · 5 min read
Sources reviewed 25 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Separate a hypothetical gross beneficiary payment from ordinary RDSP assistance repayment

Interactive planning lab

Gross beneficiary payment before any tax$2,500
Separate government assistance repayment from the plan$7,500
RDSP value after both modeled outflows$90,000

An ordinary-rule illustration for a DTC-eligible beneficiary before the calendar year in which they turn 60, with no specified disability savings plan or other exception. It assumes the issuer has independently confirmed that the proposed payment is permitted and has supplied the applicable assistance holdback amount (AHA). Government repayment is the least of three times gross payment, pre-payment plan fair market value and the entered AHA. Input bounds keep assets sufficient and the pre-payment AHA fully covered after the beneficiary payment; they are illustration limits, not program limits. No assistance entitlement, ten-year date calculation, annual payment limit, loss of DTC status, plan closure, death, tax, withholding, fee, benefit interaction or investment return is calculated. All outflows are treated as one completed transaction with no intervening changes. The beneficiary payment leaves the RDSP but may remain an outside asset; combined plan outflow is not automatically household wealth lost.

The central idea

A beneficiary payment and a government assistance repayment are different outflows. Read each destination separately before interpreting the reduction in the RDSP balance.

01

Identify where each dollar leaving the plan goes

A withdrawal-related reduction in a Registered Disability Savings Plan (RDSP) balance need not equal the money directed to the beneficiary. A permitted payment can be accompanied by a separate repayment of government grants and bonds. Those two destinations should remain visible in the household’s cash plan.

Employment and Social Development Canada’s withdrawal guidance explains that certain withdrawals can trigger assistance repayment. The illustration here isolates an ordinary proportional-repayment case for a beneficiary who remains eligible for the Disability Tax Credit (DTC), before the calendar year in which they turn sixty.

It assumes that the issuer has separately confirmed the proposed payment is permitted. It does not decide whether someone can withdraw, establish an annual payment limit or cover specified disability savings plans, loss of DTC eligibility, closure or death. Those conditions can change the applicable treatment and need their own review.

02

Use the applicable assistance holdback amount rather than lifetime grants

The assistance holdback amount, or AHA, is a defined measure of recent government assistance, reduced by relevant amounts already repaid. It is not simply every grant and bond ever received, and it is not automatically the entire RDSP balance.

The default example enters an assumed issuer-confirmed AHA of CAD 10,000 and a plan fair market value of CAD 100,000. These are invented records for teaching. The calculator does not derive the holdback from account age, contribution history or a presumed final grant date.

Payment dates and prior repayments matter when an issuer determines the applicable amount. The ordinary definition refers to the preceding ten-year period, while special circumstances require separate treatment. A single balance field cannot establish that a particular assistance payment has aged out.

The controls’ limits are illustration boundaries, rather than RDSP program limits. They keep sufficient plan assets in every displayed case so that the selected gross payment and assistance repayment can be reconciled without a negative plan value.

03

Apply the ordinary repayment calculation to the hypothetical payment

For the scoped ordinary case, section 5.3 of the Canada Disability Savings Regulations sets repayment as the least of three amounts: three dollars per dollar of the disability assistance payment, pre-payment plan fair market value and the applicable AHA.

The gross beneficiary payment is CAD 2,500. Three times that amount is CAD 7,500, below both the CAD 10,000 entered AHA and CAD 100,000 opening value. The modeled assistance repayment is consequently CAD 7,500.

The beneficiary payment and assistance repayment together remove CAD 10,000 from the plan. Subtracting those two outflows leaves CAD 90,000 in the RDSP. The waterfall traces each destination rather than presenting the whole CAD 10,000 reduction as cash paid to the beneficiary.

This calculation assumes the ordinary rule applies. It does not convert an entered request into an authorized payment or replace the issuer’s application of other payment conditions.

04

Read the cap without treating several scenarios as repeated payments

The line chart varies a single gross beneficiary payment against the same hypothetical starting record. Assistance repayment initially rises at three times the gross payment, until the entered AHA caps it. The combined plan outflow includes both the payment and repayment.

With the default CAD 10,000 AHA, the cap is reached at a gross payment of CAD 10,000 divided by three. The plot includes that exact turning point, rather than drawing a smoothed curve that obscures the change in slope.

Each point is an alternative single transaction. It is not a sequence of withdrawals that each starts again with CAD 10,000 of holdback. In the selected CAD 2,500 example, repaying CAD 7,500 reduces the entered AHA to CAD 2,500 immediately after the modeled repayment, assuming no intervening changes.

The grouped bars compare different hypothetical starting AHAs while holding the selected payment constant. Actual subsequent payments require an updated issuer record, including any new assistance, aging or other relevant event.

05

Distinguish plan outflow from household wealth lost

For a small payment while the three-for-one rule is uncapped, CAD 1 directed to the beneficiary can be accompanied by CAD 3 repaid to government. The matrix describes this as CAD 4 leaving the RDSP for each CAD 1 of gross beneficiary payment.

That is a measure of plan outflow, rather than CAD 4 of household wealth automatically disappearing. If the beneficiary retains the CAD 1 outside the RDSP, it remains a household asset. In the default example, CAD 90,000 remains in the plan and CAD 2,500 is directed outside it, totaling CAD 92,500 before any tax or other cost.

The separate CAD 7,500 government repayment explains the reduction from the original CAD 100,000 combined resources under that retained-cash assumption. Spending the beneficiary payment would create a further change outside this plan-only ledger.

A lower outflow ratio after the cap binds is not a reason to request more money. A larger payment can lower that ratio while still removing more dollars from the plan. The actual cash need and the permitted payment are separate decisions.

06

Confirm the permitted payment and spendable cash separately

A gross beneficiary payment does not establish after-tax spending cash. The payment’s composition and applicable tax treatment require separate calculation. This tool does not divide it into taxable and non-taxable portions, estimate withholding or assess effects on benefits.

The CRA’s RDSP guide discusses payment conditions and exceptions beyond the simplified ordinary case. Confirm the applicable AHA, permitted payment, repayment amount and net cash treatment with the issuer before using real amounts in a plan.

The legal consolidation consulted was current to 30 September 2026 and last amended on 29 June 2021; the sources were reviewed on 25 October 2026. Recheck the current rules and the account record for an actual transaction. The four charts explain a narrow reconciliation while keeping those unresolved eligibility and payment details outside the arithmetic.

Sources and scope

Public sources reviewed on 25 October 2026. Four original hypothetical figures isolate an ordinary proportional-repayment case using an entered assistance holdback amount. They do not determine payment eligibility, holdback dates, annual limits, tax or special-case treatment. Original scenario calculations and research checklists are TickerLantern’s educational analysis; attributed publisher examples retain their stated source and scope. Recheck current issuer documents for any product-specific decision.
